title: The Yield Curve
subtitle: The yield curve - a macroeconomic barometer
openingQuestion: What does an inverted yield curve signal?
openingOptions: A strong economy with rising short-term growth
High inflation expectations over the coming year
Nothing meaningful, just short-term market noise
A high likelihood of an upcoming recession
explanation: The yield curve connects government bond yields across different maturities, and its shape summarises the market's expectations of future interest rates. Sloping upward is the normal state. Inverted - short-term rates higher than long-term - means the market is betting that rates will have to fall, implying the economy will weaken. This is one of the few indicators with a long enough recession-forecasting track record to be worth watching, even though the lag varies a lot between episodes.

The market expects rates to fall as the economy weakens

realWorldExample.description: The US government bond yield curve inverted at its deepest and longest stretch in over 40 years during 2022-2023, as the Fed raised rates sharply to fight inflation - many economists used this signal to forecast the likelihood of a US recession.

quiz.question: What does a steep upward-sloping yield curve indicate?
options: A recession is imminent, because a steep curve signals instability
The market expects higher growth and inflation ahead
Short-term rates are much higher than long-term rates
The Fed is raising rates so the whole curve shifts up
quiz.explanation: A steep curve: a large spread between 10-year and 2-year yields → the market is optimistic about long-term growth. This happens after a recession, when the Fed has cut short-term rates but long-term rates remain elevated.

quiz.question: Why do large institutional investors watch the Yield Curve far more closely than a single interest rate level (like the 10-year rate)?
options: Because the Yield Curve is much easier to read than a single rate figure
Only central banks need to care about the Yield Curve, since private investors cannot act on it
Because the shape of the whole curve reflects expectations across many maturities at once
The Yield Curve tells you nothing a single policy rate does not already say
quiz.explanation: The Yield Curve is a 'map' of market expectations spanning many maturities - the slope, and whether the whole curve is inverted or normal, tells you much more than a single point.

quiz.question: What does an upward-sloping yield curve reflect?
options: Expected inflation is gradually declining across every long maturity on the curve
The market is forecasting a recession in the near term
The central bank is tightening monetary policy
Longer maturities demand a higher premium, a normally functioning economy
quiz.explanation: Lending for longer carries more uncertainty, so a higher yield is demanded. This is the default shape of the curve, and it reflects a normally functioning economy.

quiz.question: What is an inverted yield curve considered a signal of?
options: A recession warning, though the lag can be as long as a year
Confirmation that the economy is overheating
A sign that inflation is about to spike in the near term
A signal the central bank is about to raise rates further at its next meeting
quiz.explanation: Short-term yields exceeding long-term yields means the market is betting that rates will have to fall sharply - something that usually only happens when the economy is heading down. This indicator has been right ahead of most US recessions, but the lag is long and uneven.

quiz.question: A nearly flat yield curve usually appears at which stage?
options: The middle stage of strong, stable growth
A transitional stage, when the market hasn't settled on a direction
Right after the central bank makes a deep rate cut
A stage of high inflation persisting for several consecutive years without relief
quiz.explanation: Flat is the state between upward-sloping and inverted - the market is balancing two opposing scenarios. It often appears when a tightening cycle is nearing its end but what comes next isn't yet clear.

keyTakeaways: Yield curve: bond yields plotted by maturity
Inverted curve: signals a recession (~80% accuracy historically)
Steep curve: expectations of higher growth and inflation

practicePrompt.question: You plot a chart with government bond maturities (1 year, 5 years, 10 years, 30 years) on the horizontal axis and each maturity's corresponding yield on the vertical axis, then connect the points. What is this chart called, and what shape does it normally take?
options: This is called a Credit Spread Curve, reflecting the credit risk of each maturity
Yield curve: yields plotted by maturity; an inverted shape usually signals a recession
This is called the Efficient Frontier, showing the relationship between risk and expected return for a portfolio
This chart has no specific technical name in bond analysis

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Look up the current short-term (e.g. 2-year) and long-term (e.g. 10-year) government bond yields, and compare whether the curve is currently normal or inverted.
application.secondary: This is one of the most closely watched macroeconomic indicators in the world.

sections.text: The yield curve is a chart connecting government bond yields across maturities - from a few months to 30 years. It's not just a technical chart: it's a barometer reflecting the entire market's collective expectations of future growth, inflation, and interest rate policy.

When the curve slopes up steeply - meaning the gap between the 10-year and 2-year yield is large - the market is expecting higher growth and inflation ahead, demanding a large premium for locking up capital long-term. This usually happens after a recession, when the central bank has cut short-term rates low but long-term rates remain high because the market believes in a recovery.
Inverted curve: the most reliable recession signal

Conversely, when short-term rates exceed long-term rates (inverted), the market is betting that the central bank will soon have to cut rates to rescue a weakening economy. From 1955 to today, almost every time the US yield curve has inverted, it has preceded an actual recession by 12 to 18 months - one of the macroeconomic indicators with the highest historical accuracy. During 2022-2023, as the Fed raised rates sharply to fight 9% inflation, the US yield curve inverted at its deepest and longest stretch in over 40 years, prompting close attention from economists forecasting recession risk.

items: The yield curve is a composite picture across many maturities at once - richer in information than a single rate level
Normal curve (upward sloping): normal to high expected growth and inflation
Flat curve: market uncertainty, usually at a cycle transition point
Inverted curve: a recession warning, ~80% historical accuracy

lines: Don't look at just one rate level - the shape of the whole curve tells the full story.
The yield curve is a macro tool watched closely by both the Fed and institutional investors.
